messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marisol is a 26-year-old college student who came for treatment months after an accidental toxic chemical exposure in a campus laboratory. She had been working late, nearly alone, when a container ruptured and released fumes into the room. What she remembers most clearly is not a neat sequence but flashes: the sting in her throat and chest, the sharp smell of chemicals and cleaning agents, the fluorescent hallway outside the lab, and then being on the floor with pain moving through her body as people shouted instructions she could not follow. She was taken to the hospital, where antiseptic smells blended with the earlier fumes. Even now, when she tries to describe what happened, Marisol says she knows it occurred but cannot find words for it, and the pieces come back in the wrong order. When the memory breaks through, she feels pain again in the same parts of her body that burned during the exposure. Those disjointed, bodily memories have fed a painful conclusion: something is wrong with her, and her body cannot be trusted to tell her when she is actually safe.

In the weeks after the accident, darkness became especially potent. Walking across campus at night, entering a dim classroom before the lights came on, or waking suddenly in a dark bedroom could bring back the lab in an immediate, sensory way. The smell of antiseptic in the student health center or on freshly cleaned floors could do the same. In those moments her body seemed to react before she could think. She would go rigid, her heart pounding, muscles tightening, and if someone brushed past her unexpectedly she startled violently as if touched in the middle of the emergency. The trigger and the alarm came fused together; once her body surged into danger mode, the fragments of the event pushed in harder, still jumbled and hard to say aloud, but vivid enough to bring back the same physical pain.

Because these reminders felt so overpowering, Marisol began organizing her life around not setting them off. She stopped going near the science building where the exposure had happened, even when avoiding that route made her late to class. As a student, she now arrives early to claim seats near doors and scans each room for exits, ventilation, odd smells, and anything that might signal danger. At night she keeps lights on in her apartment and delays sleep until she is exhausted, because waking in darkness feels unbearable. She also tries to force the whole event out of mind, cutting off thoughts the moment they begin, telling herself she has to erase it or she will lose control. Her constant bodily tension pushes these habits further; the more on alert she feels, the more she checks and avoids, hoping to prevent another surge.

Her beliefs about herself and her body have deepened this pattern. Marisol has come to believe that her continued reactions mean she is fundamentally damaged, weaker than other people, and unable to recover normally. She is frightened by how quickly her body mobilizes—how a smell, a dark room, or an unexpected touch can make her feel endangered before she has time to orient herself—and she takes this as evidence that her body is now an enemy, unreliable and beyond her control. Because she sees her reactions this way, she watches even more closely for possible reminders and becomes wary of the very conditions that might set her off: dark spaces, nighttime awakenings, the sterile smell of hospitals or disinfectant. She avoids the lab building not only because it reminds her of the event, but because she is certain that if her body starts reacting there, she will not be able to manage it.

The memory itself keeps reinforcing these conclusions. When she cannot put the story in order or find words for key moments, she hears this as proof that something inside her has been altered. When pain returns with the memory, she feels certain her body is still carrying the exposure and may fail her again without warning. That fear keeps her physically braced, and in that state she notices every flicker of darkness, every chemical or antiseptic scent, every unexpected approach by another person. Ordinary campus life has narrowed around these calculations. Group study sessions run late are declined. She avoids evening events and has started missing academic opportunities if they require time in the building where the accident occurred. Friends have told her she seems far away and jumpy, but she pulls back rather than explain, because the more she tries to tell the story, the more confused and wordless she becomes.

What finally brought Marisol to seek help was a recent night when she woke in a dark room during a brief power outage, bolted upright in pain and panic, and recoiled when her roommate touched her shoulder. Afterward she was shaken by how completely her body had taken over and by how quickly the hospital smell from a first-aid kit sent the whole scene rushing back. She came in afraid that this is who she is now—defective, unsafe in her own body, and one trigger away from losing control again—but also hoping that if she can finally make sense of what happened, she might not have to keep living as if the exposure is still happening.
